events.text: Dark, and close, and warm in one place, and the warm place is you. All round you the yellow clay is packed hard and cool, the way earth is at the end of summer. Above, through a forearm of ground, there are feet. Somebody is pacing out a house: four steps, turn, four steps, turn. The old people say no one should dig in the eighteen days before autumn. Somebody is digging anyway.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to the feet

effects.log: Four steps, turn. Four steps, turn. The feet walk a square round you, and stop in the middle of it, right over you, and stand there a long time. Whoever it is does not know why that spot feels like the place to stand. You do.

choices.text: Draw warmth in from the clay around you

effects.log: The warmth comes in from every side, slowly, the way heat comes out of a hearthstone. You are the size of a fist. By morning you are the size of a slightly larger fist. It is a start.

choices.text: Beat once, slowly

effects.log: Once. The feet above you stop. A long pause. Then they move off quickly, and you hear someone say to someone else that the ground is strange in this spot, and someone else say that all ground is strange in the dead days, and to keep pacing.

events.text: Four posts, one at each corner of the site, sunk in four holes. Each blow of the mallet comes down through the clay to you like a knock at a door. On the fourth post an old neighbour shouts over the fence: it is the dead days, the earth is asleep, and whoever wakes it will take sick from the moved ground. The builder laughs and goes on knocking.

choices.text: Let the posts settle into the clay, and hold them

effects.log: You lean the whole site toward its middle, gently, the way a bowl leans toward its bottom. The four posts go in straight and stay straight. Eighty years later they will still be straight, and nobody will ever know why the house never sagged.

choices.text: Send a shiver up the fourth post

effects.log: The post hums in the builder's hands like a struck bell. The mallet goes down in the dirt. The old neighbour says nothing, very loudly. That evening the builder pours a bowl of rice into the fourth hole before the post goes in. You accept it.

choices.text: Sleep through the knocking

effects.log: Knock, knock, knock. It is not your door yet. You sleep, warm, while a house is put up round you, and wake under a roof you did not see built.

events.text: A spade, coming down. They are digging the shallow pit for the hearth-stone of the main room, and they have dug it, without knowing, right over the centre of the site. Each bite of the blade is closer. The next one stops a finger's width above you, on a stone you did not know was there.

choices.text: Stay still and hope the stone holds

ok.log: The stone holds. The digger grunts, decides the pit is deep enough, and sets the hearth-stone in it. For the rest of the life of that house its fire burns over you. Your first winter is very warm.

fail.log: The stone turns. The edge of the spade comes down and takes a crumb of you away, and you feel it the way a sleeper feels a cold hand. The digger looks at the spade. The clay on it is warm as new bread. The digger scrapes it back into the pit and does not mention it at supper. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go cold, so you feel like any other clay

effects.log: You let your warmth sink down and away until you are cool as the ground round you. The spade bites, finds nothing but clay, and stops. It is the first thing you learn: the safest way to be the centre is to feel like the edge.

choices.text: Let the digger feel you

effects.log: The digger kneels and puts a palm flat on the clay, and takes it away, and puts it back. Warm. Warm the way an animal is warm. The digger sits back on both heels for a long time, then pats the earth flat over you, very carefully, and that autumn there is a jar.

events.text: The first rain. It comes at the end of the dead days, all at once, and the new roof does not cover the whole yard yet. You feel it soak down from above: the top of the clay going dark, then the next hand's depth, then the next, a slow cold coming down toward you like news.

choices.text: Drink it slowly, the way old earth does

effects.log: You let it reach you a drop at a time and take each one in. By morning you are heavier and softer and much more yourself. You will drink every rain this way for the rest of your life, and there will be a great many rains.

choices.text: Let it run round you and on down

effects.log: It parts round you like a stream round a stone and goes on into the deep ground, to the place where the wells get their water. You stay dry and warm in the middle of it. A centre is the place the water goes round.

choices.text: Hold the rain back from the new posts

effects.log: You draw the wet toward yourself and away from the four post-holes. The posts stay dry at the foot. You are soaked through and cold for a month. The house never rots at its corners.

events.text: In the warm dark you remember a weight you have never carried. Someone, somewhere, in a life that was not yours, stood in an empty centre for a whole season and held everything that leaned on it, every harvest and every war, to the last day, and did not set it down. You are born with the shape of it in you, like a groove worn in a step.

choices.text: Fit yourself to the groove

effects.log: It fits. You are smaller than the groove by a very long way, and you will grow toward it all your life. Whoever held it to the end left you a promise: the first time you try to set something down, it will not fall.

choices.text: Wonder why anyone would hold it so long

effects.log: Pride, perhaps. Or kindness. Or simply not knowing how to stop. You turn it over all winter in the clay. You do not find out. You do notice that you are already very good at not moving.

events.text: A question comes to you in the clay, from a long way off, in a voice that is not yours: who is supposed to be standing here? Someone asked it over and over in an empty centre, in a life that was not yours, until somebody answered. You do not know the answer. You know that, somewhere very far above, four of them know your name.

choices.text: Ask it again, softly, into the clay

effects.log: Who is supposed to be standing here? The clay does not answer. The clay is very old and very patient and has heard every question. It goes on being warm round you, which is a kind of answer, if you are a clod.

choices.text: Keep the question for later

effects.log: You fold it up small and keep it at your middle, where you keep everything. A very long time from now, at the end of a road you cannot see, someone will be waiting to hear you ask it.

events.text: The tenth month, the best month. The family digs a little hollow in the ground behind the house, by the soy-sauce jars, right over you, and sets a jar of new rice in it. Over the jar they put a straw cap, woven in a cone like a tiny thatched roof. The rice is cold. Then it is less cold. Then it is warm, because you are under it.

choices.text: Warm the rice all through

effects.log: Every grain, to the middle of the jar. In the morning a child lifts the straw cap to look and says the rice is warm, and is told not to be silly, and is told not to lift the cap again, which is how you know the child was right.

choices.text: Listen to what they say over it

effects.log: "For the old lord of the site," says the eldest, and the others say it after. They do not know your name. They have a word for the place you are, and it turns out the place has always had someone in it. You are the someone now.

choices.text: Taste the new rice

effects.log: It goes into you the way warmth goes into cold hands. It tastes of the whole summer: the flooded paddies, the weeding, the backs bent in the sun. You did not know you were hungry. You are the household's now, and it is yours.

events.text: {npc}, the grandmother of the house, comes out before dawn with a bowl of clear water, sets it on the flat stone by the jar, and bows. Palms together, rubbing slowly. {He} asks for nothing grand: that the children do not take the fever going round, that the ox lives through the winter, that the roof holds. Then {he} bows again and goes in.

choices.text: Warm the jar under those old hands

mem.note: warmed the jar under my hands at dawn

effects.log: The hands stop on the cap. They stay a long time. Then {npc} bows a third time, lower than the first two, and goes in without a word to anyone. From then on {he} bows three times.

choices.text: Stay still: a site spirit should not show off

effects.log: Nothing happens, which is what is supposed to happen. {npc} goes in. The children do not take the fever. The ox lives. The roof holds. {He} never knows it was you, and that is the right way round.

choices.text: Send {him} a good dream

effects.log: That night {npc} dreams of a yellow field going all the way to the edge of the sky, and wakes laughing. {He} tells the whole house at breakfast. Nobody else understands why it was a good dream. {He} does.

events.text: The tenth month comes round again. The family lifts the straw cap, tips the old year's rice out into a basket, and pours in the new. The old rice goes to the kitchen to be steamed into rice cakes. The new rice comes down into the jar with a sound like a long breath let out.

choices.text: Let the old rice go with a blessing

effects.log: A year of you is in that rice. The family eats it in steamed cakes, all together, and for the rest of the winter they are very hard to make ill. Luck, it turns out, can be eaten.

choices.text: Keep a little warmth back in the old grains

effects.log: You keep a breath of the old year in yourself before it goes. Not much. A centre has to keep something, or it is only a hole things fall through.

choices.text: Reach up into the new rice at once

effects.log: You go up into the new grains like roots into new soil, all at once, hungrily. The jar is warm by noon. A year begins.

events.text: The fever that went through the village went round this house. The hail that broke the barley on the next field stopped at the line of this one. The neighbour's ox died in the cold and this ox did not. You begin to notice that these are not accidents. They are going out of you, a little at a time, into the house above.

choices.text: Keep giving, and ask nothing about it

effects.log: It costs you something every time. You do not ask how much. The house above you has a good year, and another, and you are a little thinner each spring and a little fuller each tenth month. That is the arrangement. Nobody made it. It is the arrangement anyway. (-3 health)

choices.text: Feel carefully for what it costs

effects.log: A child's fever: a night of your warmth. An ox through the winter: most of a month. A hailstorm turned aside: you are cold until spring. It is a measure, like rice in a ladle. You learn to count.

choices.text: Send a little over the fence to the neighbour's field

effects.log: Just a little, along the root of the hedge. The neighbour's barley stands the next hail. Your own house has a slightly worse year and never knows it. The grandmother says the old lord of the site must be getting generous in age.

events.text: {npc} is old now. {He} brings a grandchild out to the jar at dawn, holding the small hand flat over the straw cap, and teaches the bow: palms together, three times, and the water in the bowl must be clear. "When I am not here," {he} tells the jar, not the child, "look after them anyway. They will forget the water sometimes. Look after them anyway."

choices.text: Promise

mem.note: warmed the jar when I asked

effects.log: The jar goes warm under the two hands, the old one and the small one. The child gasps. {npc} only nods, as if a bargain has been struck at market. You will keep it longer than either of them can imagine.
effects.npcPass: old age, in the farmhouse, a grandchild at her side

choices.text: Warm only the child's hand

effects.log: The small hand jerks back. The child stares. {npc} laughs, the first laugh in a long time, and says: "There. Now you have met." The child will bow three times every morning for years.
effects.npcPass: old age, in the farmhouse, a grandchild at her side

choices.text: Stay still and let the old one believe what is easy

effects.log: Nothing happens under their hands. {npc} bows anyway, and the child copies, badly, and they go in. Faith does not need the jar to be warm. You will look after them anyway. You had already decided.
effects.npcPass: old age, in the farmhouse, a grandchild at her side

events.text: Kimjang: the whole house salting cabbages for three days, red to the elbows. Then they dig holes in the ground beside your jar and bury the big kimchi jars to the neck, so the winter will keep them cold but not frozen. Six fat jars, all round you, like guests who arrived early and mean to stay till spring.

choices.text: Keep them warm through the frost

effects.log: Too warm. By the New Year the kimchi is sour enough to make the grandfather's eyes water and the children shout. The grandmother says the ground behind the house has always been odd. They eat it anyway. Sour kimchi in a hard winter is still kimchi.

choices.text: Be as cold as ordinary earth

effects.log: You draw your warmth in close, to your own jar only, and let the ground round the guests be the ground. The kimchi ripens as kimchi should. Being useful, you are learning, is sometimes a matter of doing nothing in particular very carefully.

choices.text: Try to keep each jar exactly right

ok.log: Six jars, six warmths, all slightly different, held all winter. The kimchi of this house is the best in the valley that year, and the neighbours come asking what the trick is. "The ground," says the grandmother. She is right and does not know it.

fail.log: Five jars right and one frozen through. The family digs it up in the thaw and finds the cabbage cracked with ice. You are absurdly ashamed. The ox gets that jar, and is delighted. (-4 health)

events.text: Snow on the jangdokdae. Late at night the kitchen door slides open a crack, and a child of the house creeps out barefoot through the snow to the buried jars, lifts a straw lid, and eats cold kimchi with bare fingers in the moonlight, shivering and very happy.

choices.text: Warm the snow under those bare feet

effects.log: The snow under the child's feet goes soft and almost warm. The child does not notice, which is how a child should be looked after. In the morning there are little footprints round the jar, already melted into puddles. The grandmother sees them and says nothing.

choices.text: Make the lid creak, so the child runs back to bed

effects.log: Creak. The child bolts, red-fingered, and dives back under the quilt with a heart going like a drum. The child will not do it again for nearly a week.

choices.text: Keep watch until the door slides shut

effects.log: You do nothing. You only watch, all the way back to the door. A centre is mostly that: the place from which somebody is watched safely home.

events.text: Spring. The kimchi jars come up out of the ground one by one, empty, and the yard behind the house is left full of six round holes, like a face after a smile. The family fills them back in with whatever earth is handy. Some of it is yours.

choices.text: Take the loose earth back into yourself

effects.log: It comes back to you a spadeful at a time, cold and disturbed and smelling of garlic. You warm it and settle it. By summer you cannot tell which earth was ever moved. That is one of your gifts: you make moved ground forget it was moved.

choices.text: Leave the holes soft for the hens to bathe in

effects.log: The hens find them at once. All summer six hens sit in six warm hollows in the dust behind the house, looking very pleased with themselves. They are the first creatures to love you for exactly what you are.

events.text: A thin year. The rains came late and the harvest came small, and in the tenth month only half a jar of new rice goes over you. You feel the gap at once, a cold space in the top of the jar where grain should be. The luck goes up out of you as it always does. Less comes down.

choices.text: Give as much as always, from your own warmth

effects.log: The house has an ordinary year, which in a thin year is a miracle nobody notices. You spend the winter colder than you have ever been, curled tight round the bottom of the jar. Spring is a long time coming. (-5 health)

choices.text: Give only what the rice gives you

effects.log: Half a jar, half a year of luck. The house scrapes through, with a cough or two and a hen lost to a weasel. It is fair. It does not feel fair. You begin to understand that the two are different things.

choices.text: Reach deeper into the clay for more

effects.log: Down, past where you have been, into old cold ground. There is warmth there, very slow and very deep, the warmth of the whole valley. You draw a little up. It is like drinking from a well with a long rope. It will be a long time before you can draw much.

events.text: The old rice from your jar is steamed into rice cakes in a clay steamer, and the family eats them in the main room with the door shut. Not one goes over the wall to the neighbours, though every other cake of the tenth month does. "The old lord of the site is greedy," the grandmother explains to a child. "What is the site's stays in the house."

choices.text: Be as greedy as they say

effects.log: Very well. What is yours stays yours. The house gets every scrap of luck you have, and the neighbours get none, and the walls of this yard are a border. It is a very old way to be a spirit. It works. It is not very warm.

choices.text: Sulk: you never asked for that

effects.log: You never once asked anyone to hide their rice cakes. Somebody decided long ago what a site spirit wants, and here you are, being it. You sulk under the jar all winter. Nobody notices a sulking clod. That is the worst part.

choices.text: Warm the steamer so the cakes come out too many to finish

effects.log: Somehow the steamer gives a whole layer more than it should. The family cannot finish them. The grandmother looks at the heap for a long time and then, very slowly, sends a plate over the wall. Nothing bad happens. The next year she sends two.

events.text: One winter you find the bottom of yourself. You gave and gave, a fever here, a frost turned there, and one morning there is nothing left to send up. The jar above you is cold. The family does not know. The grandmother touches the cap at dawn and frowns, just a little, and goes in.

choices.text: Lie fallow until the new rice

effects.log: You give nothing for two months. A child coughs for a week. A hen stops laying. Nothing worse. The new rice comes in the tenth month, and you fill up from it like a dry field from the first rain. Luck is something you can run out of. You will remember.

choices.text: Scrape up the last of yourself and send it anyway

ok.log: There was more at the bottom than you thought. There always is, once. The house has its good winter. You know now exactly how deep the bottom is, and you will never be quite so careless near it again.

fail.log: There was nothing at the bottom but cold. You send it anyway, and it is nothing, and you spend the rest of the winter a hard grey lump of ordinary clay, barely warm. In spring you are slow to come back. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ask the clay round you for a loan

effects.log: The clay gives you a little, the way old earth gives anything: slowly and with no interest asked. You pay it back in summer. It is the first time you learn that a centre is held up too, by everything round it.

events.text: Something is eating your rice. You feel it first as a tiny theft, grain by grain, from the top of the jar at night. Then you hear it: teeth, very fast, in the straw cap. A rat has gnawed a door through the roof of your jar and is sitting in your rice, eating it, with the confidence of something that has never been caught.

choices.text: Shake the jar

effects.log: The whole jar shudders. The rat goes out through its door so fast it leaves half a whisker behind. You feel very powerful for almost a whole night, until you hear it come back, more slowly, to see what that was.

choices.text: Let it eat

effects.log: It eats until its belly is round, and then curls up in the rice and goes to sleep, right over you, warm. It is the first creature to sleep on you on purpose. You find you do not mind at all.

choices.text: Make the rice too warm to touch

effects.log: The rat puts its paw in the rice and takes it out again very quickly. It looks at the rice. It puts its nose in. It takes its nose out. It sits on the rim of the jar, deeply offended, and washes its paws for a long time before it goes.

events.text: The rat is back. It is winter and the storehouse is shut tight and the cat of the house is fat and patient, and the rat has come to the only door it knows that never closes. It sits on the rim of your jar, thin, its ribs going fast, and looks down into the rice, and does not come in. It is waiting to see what you will do.

choices.text: Make a bargain: a little rice, for keeping the other rats out

effects.log: It understands. Rats understand bargains better than most people. All winter it eats a little from the top of the jar and chases off every other rat in the yard with a fury that is wonderful to feel. Your rice has never been better guarded.

choices.text: Drive it off toward the storehouse

effects.log: It goes, slowly, looking back. The storehouse is the house serpent's ground, and the cat's. You do not hear it again that winter. In spring you think about it more than you expected to.

choices.text: Let it in and say nothing

effects.log: You do nothing, and it understands that too. It comes in out of the cold and eats, and sleeps in the straw cap where the warmth collects. By spring it is fat and glossy and has started to think of the jar as its own. Tenants are like that.

events.text: Rats do not live long. This one is old now, grey round the nose, slow on the rim of the jar. It still comes. It sits in the straw cap through the long nights and makes small sounds, and you have begun, without deciding to, to answer them with small warmths. You have nobody else to talk to. Neither does the rat.

choices.text: Talk with it all winter

effects.log: It tells you about the cat, the storehouse, the hole under the kitchen step, the grandmother's slipper that misses every time. You tell it about rain, and roots, and the deep warmth under the valley. Neither of you understands a word. It is the best winter you have had.

choices.text: Keep the straw cap warm when the end comes

effects.log: On a cold night in the second month it curls up in the warmest part of the cap and does not wake. You keep that spot warm for a week after. Nobody will ever know that the first friend of the old lord of the site was a rat. You will.

choices.text: Let it go out into the yard one last time

effects.log: It goes down off the jar on a mild night and across the yard, slowly, nose up, the way old things go to look at the world once more. It does not come back. In spring there is a nest of young rats under the kitchen step. None of them knows you. That is how it should be.

events.text: Something long and cool comes along the line of the soy-sauce jars one evening and stops by yours. A rat snake, thick as a wrist, its scales the colour of old straw. It does not hunt. It tastes the air over your jar with a black tongue for a long time. This is the house serpent of the storehouse, the one the family leaves rice for and never drives out: the luck of the grain and the coin. Two spirits. One house.

choices.text: Greet it with a little warmth

effects.log: It tastes the warmth. It considers. Then it lays its chin on the edge of the stone by your jar, for the length of a breath, the way one old neighbour leans on another's fence. It goes back to the storehouse. You have met the other luck.

choices.text: Warn it off your ground

effects.log: You go cold and hard under it, and the stones by the jar tremble. It pulls back its head and goes, unhurried, the way something goes that has been in this house longer than you have. Neither of you forgets it.

choices.text: Lie still and watch it

effects.log: It watches you back, if a snake can watch a jar. Then it goes. You lie awake all night thinking about the storehouse, and the grain, and the coin, and which of you the house really owes its good years to.

events.text: A good harvest, the best in years. The grandmother leaves a bowl of rice at the storehouse door for the serpent, and a bowl of clear water on the stone by your jar, and that night you can feel the serpent in the dark of the storehouse, coiled on the full sacks, quietly certain that the harvest was its doing.

choices.text: Let it have the credit

effects.log: It was the rain, mostly, and the family's backs. You may have helped. The serpent may have helped. You let it be proud of the sacks. Somebody in a house ought to be proud of the sacks.

choices.text: Propose a division: it keeps the grain and the coin, you keep the people

effects.log: Things and people. It tastes the idea for a whole season, and then, one morning, there is a shed skin laid along the stones by your jar, whole and pale as paper. That is a yes, from a snake. You keep the fevers off; it keeps the weevils out.

choices.text: Send the next good luck somewhere it can see, to make the point

effects.log: The grandfather finds a silver hairpin in the yard, lost by some traveller, right on top of your patch of ground. The family talks about it for a month. In the storehouse, something long and cool is not amused.

events.text: A son of the house, new to farming and full of himself, found the serpent sunning on the storehouse step and threw a stone at it, and laughed. The serpent is leaving. You feel it going along the back wall, slowly, toward the gap in the hedge. Everybody in the valley knows what it means when the house serpent goes: the luck of the grain goes with it.

choices.text: Beg it to stay

ok.log: You warm the ground in front of it, all along the hedge, a path of warmth back to the storehouse. It stops. It lies in the warmth a long time. At dusk it turns round. The son of the house has a bad fever that winter, and gets well, and never throws a stone at anything again.

fail.log: It lies in the warmth for a moment, then goes on through the hedge. A snake keeps its own counsel. By the next harvest the storehouse is half empty, and the family does not know why. You do.

choices.text: Let it go, and carry the grain-luck yourself

effects.log: It goes. You reach across the yard into the storehouse, where you have never reached, and hold up the sacks as well as the people. It is twice the weight. You are twice as tired. The storehouse stays only a little emptier than it should. (-5 health)

choices.text: Make the son of the house sorry

effects.log: The young man's feet go cold as river stones every time he crosses the yard, all autumn, until the grandmother takes him to the storehouse step with a bowl of rice and makes him bow to it. The serpent, watching from the hedge, comes home. It is not grateful. Snakes are not.

events.text: The house serpent is very old now. It comes out on the warm stones by your jar more and more, in the late afternoons, and lies there with its eyes open and its long body loose. The two lucks of one house, side by side in the sun. The grandmother sees it from the kitchen door and goes very quiet, and does not shoo the hens near it.

choices.text: Ask it, at last, which of you the house owes more

effects.log: It does not answer for a whole afternoon. Then it slides its head onto the rim of your jar and leaves it there. You decide that means: both, and neither, and what a question. You never ask again.

choices.text: Keep the stones warm for it every afternoon

effects.log: All summer the stones by your jar are the warmest in the valley. The old serpent lies on them until the light goes. When it does not come one day, the stones are warm anyway, and stay warm a little longer than they need to.

events.text: Years after the house serpent left, something comes in through the gap in the hedge at dusk: a weasel, quick and red and nervous, with a mouse in its mouth. It looks at the storehouse. It looks at your jar. It goes into the storehouse. The grandmother, at the kitchen door, puts both hands over her mouth.

choices.text: Welcome it in for the house

effects.log: A weasel can be the luck of the grain too, in some valleys. You warm the storehouse step for it all winter. By spring it is fat and fierce and the weevils are gone, and the grandmother leaves it rice. The other luck has come back, in a different coat.

choices.text: Let it find its own way

effects.log: It stays a winter and goes in spring. A weasel does not keep a house the way a serpent does. You hold up the grain alone again, and you are used to it now. That is what happens to a centre: it gets used to it.

events.text: The first full moon of the year, and the noise. It comes up the lane like weather: the little gong going like a hailstorm, the hourglass drum, the barrel drum, the big gong's long voice. A whole farmers' band comes through the gate and into the yard and begins to dance, and to stamp, stamp, stamp on the ground, singing to the earth spirit to lie down and be quiet. You are the earth spirit. It hurts.

choices.text: Endure it

effects.log: Stamp, stamp, stamp, round the yard, round the kitchen, round the jars. You lie flat under it like a field under hail. They go at last, to the next house. You ache for a week. (-4 health)

choices.text: Shake back in anger

effects.log: The ground bucks once under the big gong. A drummer goes down on one knee. The band stops dead in the moonlight. Then the leader laughs, too loudly, and shouts that the earth spirit is strong in this house, and they stamp harder. It is a long night.

choices.text: Listen to the words they are singing

effects.log: Under the drums, the words: lord of the site, lie easy, lie long; keep out the fever, keep in the grain; we press you down so you hold us up. It is not an attack. It is not quite a prayer. It is something in between that you do not have a word for yet.

events.text: The band again, the next first full moon. This time you notice the rest of it: the family waiting at the gate with a table of rice and a jug, the grandmother giving a measure of grain to the band's sack, the children running behind the drummers. The whole village goes from house to house, stamping on every yard. Not only yours. Everyone's ground.

choices.text: Feel the other yards through the clay

effects.log: Under every yard in the village there is a warmth, faint, sleeping: the site of every house. None of them is like you. All of them are being stamped on tonight, and none of them minds. You begin to suspect you have been taking it personally.

choices.text: Watch the children copying the stamp

effects.log: A row of small feet behind the band, stamping out of time, with enormous seriousness. One falls over. It gets up and stamps the ground it fell on, hard, to show it who is boss. You decide you like the children best.

choices.text: Hold still and take every stamp as it comes

effects.log: It still hurts. It hurts less. You notice that each stamp is a little different, the way each knock on a door is, and that most of them are friendly.

events.text: The band comes into the yard over you, now, not behind the house: the threshing yard is yours. The leader raises the little gong, and the whole band stamps as one, so hard the frost jumps off the straw mats. And you understand it at last. This is how humans say hello to the ground. Every year. They have been saying hello, and waiting.

choices.text: Stamp back, once

effects.log: Once. The whole yard comes up a hair's breadth under their feet and goes down again. Every drum stops. Then the big gong, very slowly, begins again, and the band dances as they have never danced in this yard, and the leader is weeping and grinning. The ground has answered.

choices.text: Hum up through their feet

effects.log: A warmth, a hum, up through the soles of every dancer at once. They do not stop; they dance faster. A child says the ground is singing. Nobody laughs. They go to the next house afterwards very quiet, smiling to themselves.

choices.text: Not yet: let them dance

effects.log: You let them stamp and go. You are not ready to answer. They will come back next year. They always come back.

events.text: The morning after the first full moon. The band's old drummer, {npc}, comes back to the yard alone, in straw sandals, with the drum on a strap and no drumstick. {He} walks to the middle of the threshing yard, where it happened last night, and stamps once, softly. And waits, head on one side.

choices.text: Answer, softly

effects.log: A small warmth under one straw sandal. {npc} closes {his} eyes. "Forty years," {he} says to the ground, "I have been knocking on yards. You are the first to open the door." {He} sits down in the middle of the yard and stays till noon.

choices.text: Stay silent: it was for the band, not for one

effects.log: {npc} waits a long time. Then {he} nods, as if the silence were an answer too, and goes. That year the band plays a little better at every house. {He} tells nobody. {He} does not need to.

events.text: {npc} is too old to dance now. {He} sits on a straw mat at the edge of the threshing yard on the first full moon and beats the barrel drum sitting down, while a grandchild leads the band, badly and with great energy. Between two songs the old drummer leans down and puts a palm flat on the ground.

choices.text: Warm the palm

mem.note: warmed the yard under my old palm

effects.log: The hand stays a long time. Then {npc} laughs and plays the next song too fast, and the young leader has to run to keep up, and the whole village laughs. It is the last year {he} comes. It is a good last year.

choices.text: Stamp once with the young leader's foot

effects.log: The young leader's heel comes down and the ground answers it, a single knock from below. The young leader freezes. {npc}, on the mat, nods once, as if handing something over. The band has a new drummer who believes.

events.text: First full moon. The band comes up the lane with its gongs and its drums, the same songs, new feet, and stamps round the yard and the kitchen and the jars, telling the earth spirit to lie easy and hold the house up.

choices.text: Answer with a little warmth

effects.log: A warmth under every stamp. The dancers grin at each other. The band says this is the best yard in the valley for jisinbapgi, and they are right.

choices.text: Lie easy, as they ask

effects.log: You lie easy. They press you down so you will hold them up. It is a fair arrangement, and the drums are good.

events.text: The dead days before autumn, and a neighbour digs a well. Right at the edge of the site, a spade going down through the yellow clay toward the water, and every bite of it comes to you like a cut. The old people say whoever moves the earth in these days will take sick of it. Over the fence, the grandmother is saying so, loudly.

choices.text: Punish the digger, as the old people say

effects.log: The digger's right arm swells by evening and will not lift a spade. The well stops at chest depth. The whole village nods and says: the dead days. You feel stronger, and a little ashamed, and stronger.

choices.text: Forgive it: the summer was dry and they need the water

effects.log: You take the cuts and say nothing. The well is dug. The water is a little bitter, because it comes up through earth that was hurt. The neighbour drinks it and is glad of it. (-3 health)

choices.text: Move the water yourself so the well comes up sweet

ok.log: You lean the deep water toward the spade, slowly, through the clay. At the next bite the hole fills, clear and cold and sweet. The digger sits in the mud laughing. The grandmother over the fence says nothing at all, which is how she admits she was wrong.

fail.log: The deep water does not move for you yet. You strain until the clay round you is hot, and the spade goes down anyway, and finds the water late and bitter. You are tired for a month. (-6 health)

events.text: The neighbour whose arm swelled comes to the edge of the site with a bowl of steamed rice cakes and a jug of clear water, and kneels, and bows to the ground over the fence, and asks the old lord of the site to forgive a fool who could not wait eighteen days. The arm is still thick and stiff. The well is still half dug.

choices.text: Lift the sickness

effects.log: The arm goes down by the next morning. The neighbour finishes the well after the turn of the season, and leaves a cake at the fence every autumn after. You find you like being apologised to. You resolve not to like it too much.

choices.text: Keep it a little longer, as a lesson

effects.log: One more month. The neighbour learns it. So does the village. Nobody digs in the dead days again in your lifetime under this yard. You are not sure whether you have taught them wisdom or only fear. Perhaps there is less difference than you would like.

events.text: The sweet well has become the village well. Everyone comes to it now, with jars on their heads and buckets on poles, and they stand round it in the evenings and talk. It is at the edge of your site. All day, the village comes to you, without knowing, and goes away full.

choices.text: Keep it sweet

effects.log: It is never bitter, not in the driest year. People say it is the best water between the two rivers. You hold it up from underneath like a cupped hand. It is the first thing you have ever held for everyone at once.

choices.text: Listen to the talk at the well

effects.log: Who is marrying whom, whose ox is lame, which magistrate is a thief. Everything in the valley passes the well sooner or later. You learn the valley from its gossip. A centre, you are discovering, is where the news comes.

events.text: Years on, and a new house going up in the dead days, at the far end of the village. The young builder has never heard the old rule, or has heard it and laughed. The old people at the well are shaking their heads, and looking, all of them, toward the site where you lie.

choices.text: Let them see the old rule is true

effects.log: A post splits as it goes in, clean down the middle. The builder stops, white, and waits the eighteen days. The old people at the well say: you see. The rule lives another generation, because of you.

choices.text: Let it pass: the far end is not your ground

effects.log: It is not. The house goes up, the builder takes no sickness, and the old people are disappointed. You learn where your edges are. A centre that reaches everywhere is not a centre. It is a flood.

choices.text: Soften the far ground so their posts go in easy

effects.log: You reach to the very edge of yourself and make the far clay kind. The young builder finishes in four days and laughs at the old rule. The rule dies a little. A house stands. You decide that is a fair trade. (-3 health)

events.text: You have outgrown the jar. One spring you find that you are not under it any more but under everything: the whole threshing yard in front of the house, packed clay swept smooth every morning with a twig broom. Feet cross you all day. Hens scratch you. A child draws on you with a stick. You lie under all of it, wide and flat and warm, and for the first time you can feel the sky.

choices.text: Stretch to the edges of the yard

effects.log: To the gate, to the kitchen step, to the foot of the wall. It takes a whole season. When you are done, the yard dries faster after rain than any yard in the village, and the hens prefer it, and nobody asks why.

choices.text: Feel every foot that crosses you

effects.log: The grandfather's slow heavy heel. The children's bare feet, running. The ox's four careful hooves. A stranger's straw sandals, once, hesitating at the gate. You learn the house by its feet.

choices.text: Keep a little of yourself under the old jar

effects.log: You stretch out under the yard, but you leave a warm root back behind the house, under the jar. The rice there stays warm in winter. Leaving a place does not have to mean leaving it cold.

events.text: Harvest. The sheaves come in from the paddies on backs and on the ox, and are spread on straw mats on the yard, and the flails begin: long poles with a swinging arm, rising and falling, rising and falling, and the grain comes off the heads and down onto you like a warm, dry rain. Then the women toss it in the winnowing baskets and the chaff goes up gold into the wind.

choices.text: Feel the grain fall

effects.log: Thousands of grains, each one a small tap, each one a summer. You lie under the harvest and it falls on you all day. You have never been so happy, and you have no way to tell anyone.

choices.text: Hold the yard firm under the flails

effects.log: Not one grain is lost in a crack, not one flail-stroke goes soft on a wet patch. The threshing of this yard is the fastest in the village. The grandfather is very proud of his yard. He should be. Partly.

choices.text: Keep the wind steady for the winnowing

ok.log: A long, even breeze off the yard all afternoon, the perfect winnowing wind. The chaff goes up and away and the clean grain falls straight back into the baskets. The women look at each other. Nobody says it. Everybody thinks it.

fail.log: The wind does not listen to you yet. It gusts, and a basket of grain goes all over the yard, and the hens are delighted. The grandmother says something very rude about the weather. You agree with every word.

events.text: Late summer, and the whole yard is red: straw mats covered with peppers drying in the sun, the year's chili for the kimchi. The family has gone to the fields. The sky in the west goes dark, then darker, and the first fat drops hit the mats with a sound like fingers on a drum.

choices.text: Hold the rain off the yard

ok.log: You push up warmth from the whole yard, a dry heat, and the rain over the yard turns to steam before it lands. When the family comes running back from the fields, the lane is a river and the peppers are dry and hot as coals. The children dance. The old people go very quiet.

fail.log: You cannot hold a whole sky. The rain comes down on the peppers, and on you, and the family comes running, and they save most of them on the porch. You are tired and wet and the yard steams for two days. (-5 health)

choices.text: Warm the mats so the peppers dry fast afterwards

effects.log: The rain comes and goes. Afterwards the yard is warm as an oven floor, and the wet peppers are dry again by evening. Not a single one moulds. A centre cannot stop the weather. It can be kind afterwards.

choices.text: Let the rain come: the yard needs it too

effects.log: You drink. The family runs home, grumbling, and drags the mats under the eaves, and loses a few peppers. You are fat with water for a week. It was a dry summer for you too.

events.text: Winter, and the yard is the children's. They spin tops on the hard frozen clay, whipping them with little string whips; they fly kites from the corner by the gate; they make a slide of ice from the kitchen step to the wall and go down it on their backsides, shrieking, until the grandmother comes out with the broom.

choices.text: Make the ice slide perfect

effects.log: Smooth as glass, fast as a hawk, and it ends exactly at a soft heap of snow by the wall. The children talk about it for years. The grandmother, who has slid down it herself at night when nobody was watching, says nothing.

choices.text: Keep the tops spinning a breath longer

effects.log: Every top on your yard spins a little longer than it should. The children of the next house come to play here, because the tops are better. Your yard becomes the place the children go. That is not nothing.

choices.text: Keep the frost soft where the smallest one falls

effects.log: The smallest falls over a great deal. Every time, the frost under it is somehow soft. It will grow up thinking the ground is a friendly thing. It will be right.

events.text: The children draw a game on your back with a stick: squares in a row, two side by side, a round head at the top. Then they throw a flat stone into a square and hop over it on one foot, out to the head and back, and pick the stone up without putting the other foot down. They call it the four-directions game. They argue about every rule.

choices.text: Learn the rules

effects.log: It takes a whole summer, because the rules change whenever the biggest child is losing. In the end you know them better than any of the players. You are the board. A board should know the rules.

choices.text: Feel which squares the stones like to land in

effects.log: The third square, for some reason. The stones want the third square. You decide it is because the third square is right over where you are warmest, and that this is a very silly thing to be proud of. You are proud of it anyway.

events.text: The smallest child, {npc}, never wins. {His} stone always skids out of the square, and {his} one foot always comes down a hair too soon, and the bigger ones laugh. Today {he} has thrown into the far square, the hardest one, and is standing on one leg at the start, very red, very serious.

choices.text: Quietly cheat: nudge the stone back into its square

mem.note: kept my stone in the square

effects.log: The stone skids, stops on the line, and then, very gently, rolls back in. Nobody sees it but {npc}, who stares at the ground for a long time. {He} wins. {He} never wins again, because you never do it again. Once is a gift. Twice is a habit.

choices.text: Firm the ground under that one foot

effects.log: The yard under {npc}'s foot goes hard and level as a step. {He} hops out to the head and back without a wobble, picks up the stone, and turns round, astonished. The bigger children say {he} has been practising. {He} lets them think so.

choices.text: Let the game be the game

effects.log: {npc} loses again. {He} kicks the stone, and then picks it up and pockets it, and comes back the next day and loses again, and the next. In the end {he} gets good. Not because of you. You are prouder of that than of anything you could have done.

events.text: Years later. {npc} comes back into the yard grown, with a pack on {his} back for a long road, and stops at the place where the squares used to be drawn. The lines are long gone. {He} finds a flat stone, throws it, and it lands in the far square that is not there any more.

choices.text: Make the stone stay

mem.note: stayed in the stone again, years later

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud in the empty yard, alone. "It was you," {he} says to the ground. "It was always you." {He} goes off down the road with the flat stone in {his} pocket, and keeps it for life.

choices.text: Let it roll

effects.log: It skids out of the square that is not there. {npc} smiles, picks it up, and pockets it. "Never could," {he} says, and goes. You were right not to help twice. Some things should be remembered as they were.

events.text: A wedding in the yard. A table on the packed clay, with a pair of carved wooden geese on it, a hen and a cock wrapped in red and blue cloth, jujubes and chestnuts in bowls. {npc} of the house stands at one side of the table in borrowed silk, very pale, and across it stands the one from over the hill. They bow to each other, again, again.

choices.text: Keep the clouds off until the last bow

effects.log: The sky is heavy all morning. It holds. The last bow, the last cup, the last guest down the lane, and then the rain comes, soft and warm, and everyone says that is luck too. {npc} looks at the yard as if {he} knows something.

choices.text: Warm the ground under those borrowed shoes

mem.note: warmed the yard on my wedding day

effects.log: {npc} stops shaking. Across the table, the one from over the hill stops shaking too. The yard is warm as a heated floor under the straw mats. Twenty years later, {npc} will still say it was the warmest day {he} remembers.

choices.text: Watch, and learn how humans join

effects.log: Bows, cups, the wooden geese that pair once for life, chestnuts thrown for children to come. Two houses becoming one, at a table, on you. You do not understand it. You watch the whole day, so that you might.

events.text: {npc} does not come out with the bowl of clear water this morning. By noon the whole house is weeping. By evening the neighbours have come with rice and white cloth. Three days later the bier goes out of the gate on the shoulders of ten bearers, painted bright as a festival, while a leader rings a hand-bell and sings the going-away song, and the bearers answer.

choices.text: Warm the yard under the bier as it passes

effects.npcDie: old age, in the tenth month, after the new rice
effects.log: The bier crosses the yard over you, slowly, the bell ringing. You make the clay under the bearers' feet warm all the way to the gate. One of the old bearers stumbles, catches the pole, and looks down, and then looks at the jar behind the house.

choices.text: Go cold in mourning

effects.npcDie: old age, in the tenth month, after the new rice
effects.log: The jar behind the house is cold for a month. The family notices and says the old lord of the site is grieving too. They are right. It is the first time you have lost anyone. You had not known it was a thing that could happen to a clod.

choices.text: Send one last warmth up the lane after the bier

effects.npcDie: old age, in the tenth month, after the new rice
effects.log: As far as your edge goes, and a little further. The bearers say afterwards that the road was dry all the way to the hill, in a week of rain. The bell-ringer swears the ground was humming. {npc} would have bowed three times.

events.text: A child of {npc}'s, barely a year old, standing for the first time in the middle of the yard, swaying, both arms out, with the whole family round in a ring holding their breath. The child looks down at the ground, puzzled, as if the ground had said something.

choices.text: Hold very still

effects.log: You hold still as stone. The child takes one step, two, three, and sits down hard, and laughs. The family cheers. {npc} picks the child up and swings it round. You were the ground the first steps were taken on. That is a thing you get to keep.

choices.text: Warm the ground under the small feet

effects.log: The child takes four steps toward the warmth, not toward {npc}'s arms, and sits down on the warmest spot in the yard and pats it. {npc} laughs and says the child likes the ground better than the family. You keep very quiet.

events.text: {npc} and a younger sibling are quarrelling in the yard over the old father's fields: who keeps the house, who goes to clear new ground on the hill. It is late and they have both said things they cannot take back. They are standing right over you, faces red in the lantern-light, and the voices are getting louder.

choices.text: Make the ground shiver between them

effects.log: A tremor, very small, right between their feet. They both step back. They both look down. The quarrel does not end. But neither of them says the next thing, the unforgivable one. In the morning they divide the fields without speaking, and in time they speak again.

choices.text: Warm the yard until they sit down

effects.log: The night is cold and the yard is warm, and without deciding to, they both sit down on it. Sitting, it is harder to shout. By midnight they are talking about their father. By cockcrow they have decided: {npc} keeps the house, the younger one gets the better field. Both think they won.

choices.text: Let them settle it themselves

effects.log: They shout, and say it, and the younger one goes off up the hill that night and does not come back for nine years. When the younger one does come back, it is to this yard. A centre cannot stop people leaving. It can be the place they come back to.

events.text: A spotted fever has come to the valley, and {npc}'s child has it, burning, in the room over the hearth-stone, over you. {npc} has sat by the mat for three nights. On the fourth, {he} goes out behind the house in the dark and kneels by the jar and does not ask for anything, because {he} cannot find the words.

choices.text: Give the child everything you can spare

mem.note: kept the child alive through the fever

ok.log: You pour yourself up through the hearth-stone into the room, all night, a steady even warmth that draws the fever down instead of feeding it. At dawn the child is sweating and sleeping. {npc} comes out to the jar and bows until the sun is up. (-4 health)

fail.log: You give and give and the fever takes it and burns brighter. You learn that warmth is not always what a body needs. The child lives, in the end, thin and slow to mend, and you lie cold and spent for a season. (-8 health)

choices.text: Cool the hearth-stone instead of warming it

effects.log: You think, for once, instead of giving. A fever needs cool, not warm. You draw the heat down out of the room into yourself, all night, and burn with it. In the morning the child is cool and asleep. You are hot as a kiln for a week, and very pleased with yourself.

choices.text: Send {npc} the strength to sit one more night

effects.log: {npc} goes back in and sits, and does not sleep, and changes the cloth, and changes it again. The child turns the corner at dawn on {npc}'s care. You only kept the watcher awake. Sometimes that is the whole of it.

events.text: {npc} has gone grey. In the tenth month {he} brings the new rice out to the jar slowly, both hands, and pours it in, and spills a little, and bows three times, the way the grandmother did. Then {he} sits down on the step by the soy-sauce jars, the way the grandmother did, and stays there a long time in the thin sun.

choices.text: Warm the step

mem.note: warmed the step by the jar in the thin sun

effects.log: {npc} sits until the sun goes. "You were here when I was born," {he} says to nobody, "and you will be here after." {He} pats the jar and goes in. It is the most anyone in this house has ever said to you.

choices.text: Send the house one more generation of good years

effects.log: You give the year everything. The harvest is the best in a few years. {npc} lives to see a grandchild walk on the yard. You are thinner for it, and older. You have begun to measure your life in their generations.

events.text: Up in the ridge beam of the house, where a folded paper with rice and a coin in it was tied on the day the roof went up, lives the lord of the house, the one the mudang calls Seongju. One night it speaks down to you, through the posts. It says the house is its house. It says you are only the ground under its house. It says this pleasantly, the way a landlord says the rent is due.
events.arc: The Other Gods of the House

choices.text: Say the house stands on you, so it is yours

effects.log: The beam creaks all night. The posts hum. The family sleeps badly and wakes cross. In the morning the lord of the house and the lord of the site are not speaking, and the soup boils over twice. You are right. Being right is not very comfortable.

choices.text: Agree: the house is the beam's, the ground is the ground's

effects.log: The roof for the beam, the floor for you, the people for both. The ridge beam considers this and finds it very fair, which means it thinks it won. You let it. The house sleeps well. Two gods in one house is a kind of partnership.

choices.text: Ask what it does all day up there

effects.log: It holds the roof up, it says, and keeps the house's name, and watches the smoke. You hold the floor up and keep the house's luck and watch the feet. You are, it turns out, in the same trade. It is a long, friendly night.

events.text: Over the hearth, on a little shelf, a white bowl of clear water is set out fresh every morning for the kitchen goddess, Jowang, who keeps the fire. The hearth-stone of the kitchen is half over you, and its fire has been warm all these years partly because of you. This morning the cook thanks the kitchen goddess for a fire that caught first time, in the wet.
events.arc: The Other Gods of the House

choices.text: Let the kitchen goddess have the credit

effects.log: She keeps the fire; you keep the stone under it. The water bowl is hers. The warm stone is yours. Nobody bows to a hearth-stone. You find, a little to your surprise, that you do not want them to.

choices.text: Let the fire go out once, to see

effects.log: The fire will not catch. It will not catch. The cook prays to the water bowl in a panic, and you relent, and it catches. The kitchen goddess knows exactly what happened. She is cold to you for a year. Fair.

choices.text: Warm the bowl of water a little, as a greeting

effects.log: The cook finds the morning water faintly warm and pours it out at once and fetches more, frowning. The second bowl is warm too. The cook gives up. Somewhere above the hearth, someone is laughing.

events.text: Night, and a child of the house has to go to the privy, out across the corner of the yard in the dark. Everyone knows the privy goddess is short-tempered and sits counting her long hair, and must be warned with a cough before anyone goes in, or she will be startled into a rage. The child has forgotten to cough, and is halfway across the yard.
events.arc: The Other Gods of the House

choices.text: Make the ground creak so the child remembers

effects.log: A creak under a bare foot. The child stops, remembers, and coughs loudly at the privy door, three times, very politely. Whatever is inside counts on undisturbed. The child goes in and comes out and runs back to bed, safe.

choices.text: Cough for the child, through the ground

effects.log: A low sound comes up out of the yard, very like a polite cough. The child freezes, then bolts back indoors and refuses to go out again until dawn. The privy goddess, they say in the morning, has a visitor. Nobody in this house forgets to cough again.

choices.text: Stay out of it: the privy is not your ground

effects.log: It is the privy goddess's. The child goes in without a cough. There is a short, terrible silence. Then the child comes out, entirely unharmed and a little puzzled. Perhaps she was in a good mood. Perhaps she lost count. You will never know.

events.text: New Year's night. Every god of the house is awake: the lord of the ridge beam, the kitchen goddess at her water bowl, the gate god, the privy goddess with her hair, the house serpent of the storehouse, the birth grandmother in the inner room. And under all of them, under the floor and the yard and the jars, you. Somebody has to be at the bottom. Everyone else is standing on it.
events.arc: The Other Gods of the House

choices.text: Hold them all up, gladly

effects.log: The house, the gods, the family asleep, the ox, the jars. All of it on you. It is not heavy yet. It will be, one day, when what stands on you is much bigger than a farmhouse. Tonight it is only warm and crowded and good.

choices.text: Notice that nobody bows to the bottom

effects.log: They bow to the beam, the bowl, the gate, the storehouse. Nobody bows to the ground except the grandmother and the stamping troupe, once a year. And yet everything stands on it. You think about this for a long time. It is the first thought you have that is a ruler's thought.

events.text: The long rains. Forty days of it, the whole sky coming down, and the mud walls of the house begin to melt. You feel the back wall going soft at the foot, then sliding, a hand's width at a time, toward the yard. Inside, the family is asleep. The ridge beam is groaning. Something is going to come down tonight.

choices.text: Hold the whole house up until morning

ok.log: You go hard under the back wall, hard as fired brick, all night, and the wall leans and leans and does not fall. At dawn the rain stops. The family comes out and looks at a wall leaning like a tired ox, and still standing, and the grandfather sits down in the mud.

fail.log: You hold it until the hour before dawn, and then you cannot. The back wall comes down into the yard with a long soft sound. The roof stays up, just. Nobody is hurt; they were all in the front room. You lie under the wet ruin, cracked with the effort. (-12 health)

choices.text: Wake the house instead

effects.log: You send a cold shock up through every sleeping mat. The whole family wakes at once, without knowing why, and the grandmother smells the wet clay and gets them all into the front room. The back wall comes down an hour later onto empty floor. Walls can be rebuilt. You chose what could not.

choices.text: Let the wall go and hold the four posts only

effects.log: You choose. The wall is mud and straw. The posts are the house. You let the wall go and hold the four posts you held when they went in, as hard as you can. The wall slumps. The roof stays. You were right, and it was hard to watch.

events.text: After the rains, the family rebuilds the wall: clay and chopped straw mixed in a pit with water, trodden with bare feet, slapped up between boards in layers. They dig the clay from the corner of the yard. They are digging you. Not your middle, only your edge, but it is you, going up in handfuls into the new wall.

choices.text: Give the clay gladly

effects.log: A wall of you. Warm in winter, cool in summer, never cracking in the frost. The family says it is the best clay they ever dug. You are a little smaller and the house is a little more yours. (-3 health)

choices.text: Make the dug clay ordinary, and keep yourself whole

effects.log: You draw back out of the corner of the yard and let them have plain clay. The wall goes up and is a perfectly ordinary wall. You stay whole. Not everything has to be given.

events.text: The new wall has stood through many rains and not cracked. The children pressed their hands into it, low down, while it was wet, and the prints are still there, small hands at the height of a child's shoulder. A younger child of the house puts a hand into one of the old prints. It fits.

choices.text: Warm the old handprint

effects.log: The small hand in the old print, warm. The child pulls it back and stares. A grown sister laughs and says the wall has always been like that, and puts a hand flat on it too. The wall is warm all along. It has always been warm. It is you.

choices.text: Keep the wall standing, quietly

effects.log: You do nothing new. You go on doing what you have done for years: holding a wall up from underneath without being asked. It turns out most of what a centre does looks exactly like nothing.

events.text: The tenth month, and the family has called a mudang for a house rite. {npc} comes with bells and a fan, a drummer, a table of steamed rice cakes and fruit, and dances in the yard by lamplight, calling the gods of the house one by one: the lord of the ridge beam, the kitchen goddess, the gate god. Then {he} turns to the jar behind the house and calls: Old lord of the site! And waits.

choices.text: Answer

effects.log: The bells in {npc}'s hand ring on their own. The lamps lean toward the jar. {npc} goes down on both knees in the yard and says, very quietly, so that only the family hears: "It is here. It has always been here." It is the first time anyone has called you by name. It is a good name.

choices.text: Let the mudang take the credit

effects.log: Nothing rings. {npc} shakes the bells, and shouts that the old lord of the site is pleased, and the family is pleased. {npc} is not sure, and looks at the jar a long time when nobody is watching. You hold still.

choices.text: Answer with the wrong voice: the floor creaks

effects.log: Every floorboard in the house creaks at once. The family shrieks. The drummer drops the stick. {npc} laughs, delighted, and dances the rest of the rite twice as fast, and is paid double. You have been named, and you have made a mudang's reputation.

events.text: {npc}, the mudang, comes back alone a month after the rite, without bells or drum, and sits on the step by the soy-sauce jars, and talks to the jar as one talks to a client. What do you want, old lord? Rice, every year. Water, every dawn. The family to remember. What else? Tell me, and I will tell them.

choices.text: Ask that the rice cakes go over the wall to the neighbours

effects.log: {npc} listens to the warmth for a long time, and then laughs. "A generous one," {he} says. "That is rare." The next tenth month the cakes go over the wall. The village thinks the family has gone soft. The family has a very good year.

choices.text: Ask for nothing

effects.log: {npc} waits. Nothing. "Hm," {he} says. "The ones that ask for nothing are the strong ones." {He} goes, and tells the family only to keep the water fresh. {He} never charges them for a rite again.

choices.text: Ask to be stamped on more gently at the New Year

effects.log: It takes {npc} some time to understand. Then {he} laughs until {he} has to wipe {his} eyes. "I will tell the band," {he} says. "Softly, for this house." {He} does. They do not.

events.text: {npc} is old. {He} comes into the yard with a young apprentice carrying the drum, and does the rite slowly, sitting for most of it. When it comes to the old lord of the site, {he} does not call. {He} puts the apprentice's hand flat on the yard and says: feel. This one you do not call. This one is already here.

choices.text: Warm the apprentice's hand

mem.note: warmed the yard under my apprentice's hand

effects.log: The young hand jerks back. {npc} nods and goes on with the rite as if nothing had happened, which is how an old mudang teaches. The apprentice will do this rite in this yard for years and never once call you, only touch the ground.

choices.text: Warm the old mudang's hand instead, for the last time

effects.log: {npc} puts {his} own hand down beside the apprentice's, and closes {his} eyes, and smiles. "Not me," {he} says. "Teach the young one." But {he} leaves the hand there a long time. {He} does not come to the yard again.

events.text: The old people at the well have started calling the oldest man in the village the old lord of the site, because he has been there longer than anybody and sits in the same place every day and knows where everything is buried. He is ninety. He thinks it is a great honour. You are younger than he is, and you have never once sat on a stool.

choices.text: Let him have the name

effects.log: He wears it well. He settles the boundary quarrels and remembers the floods and knows whose great-grandfather owed whom. Your name, used for the person in a village who stays put and knows everything. You find you are not jealous. You are flattered.

choices.text: Warm his stool at the well, every morning

effects.log: His stool by the well is always warm when he comes to it. He tells everyone he must be the real old lord of the site, then. The village laughs. You laugh too, in your way, which is a slight warmth spreading across a yard.

events.text: New Year's morning. A child of the house comes running out across the frozen ground in a new jacket, and its sleeves are striped: blue, red, yellow, white, black, a band of each, round and round to the wrist. To keep bad luck off, the grandmother says, and for a long life. You have never seen colour before. You have only ever felt warm and cold. Now there are five of something.

choices.text: Watch the yellow band

effects.log: The middle stripe. Not first, not last. The others are on either side of it. You do not know why you cannot stop looking at it. You feel, for a moment, as if somebody has drawn a picture of you on a child's arm.

choices.text: Watch all five go round together

effects.log: Blue, red, yellow, white, black, blue, red. Round and round as the child runs. None of them is the most important. Without any one of them it would not be a sleeve. You watch until the child goes in, and think about it for years.

choices.text: Warm the ground under the running feet

effects.log: The frost goes soft. The child does not fall once all morning, which for that child is a miracle. The five colours flash across you, again and again, the first beautiful thing you have ever known was beautiful.

events.text: The child in the striped sleeves sits down on the yard to rest, one arm flung out across you. And through the cloth you feel something you have never felt before: each stripe pulls, faintly, at something in the world. The blue at the willows by the stream, waiting for spring. The red at the kitchen fire. The white at the iron of the sickle. The black at the well. And the yellow at you.

choices.text: Follow each pull to its end

effects.log: Willows, fire, iron, water, and the ground. Five things that are not the same, all pulling on one child's sleeve. The world turns on five spokes, and you are lying near the hub. You do not know any of these words yet. You know the shape.

choices.text: Pull back on the yellow

effects.log: The yellow pulls; you pull back. The child shivers and sits up and looks at its sleeve. Then it looks at the ground. Then it runs inside. You have, very gently, frightened a child with yourself. You resolve to be more careful.

choices.text: Keep all five even, so none of them pulls harder

effects.log: It is very hard, like balancing five eggs on a plate. For an afternoon all five stripes pull exactly the same, and the child sleeps on the yard in the sun as if it has never slept before. It is your first taste of a kind of work you will do for a thousand years.

events.text: The striped jacket has been worn by three children, one after another, and is thin as paper at the elbows. The mother of the house unpicks it at last for rags. She keeps one strip, the yellow, and does not know why, and in the tenth month she ties it round the straw cap of the jar.

choices.text: Keep the yellow strip bright

effects.log: It never fades, though the sun and the rain have every other cloth in the yard grey within a year. The family stops noticing. Visitors do. A strip of yellow on a rice jar, bright as the day it was dyed.

choices.text: Remember the other four

effects.log: The blue, the red, the white, the black, gone to rags and dust cloths and the stuffing of a quilt. The yellow on the jar is only one fifth of something. You will spend a very long time, later, finding the other four again.

events.text: The spring hunger: the old rice gone, the barley green in the fields and not yet ripe, two months to wait with nothing in the storehouse. The family boils pine bark and arrowroot. The children are quiet in a way children should not be. And behind the house there is one jar of rice they have not touched: yours. The mother of the house stands by it with a gourd dipper for a long time.
events.arc: The Year the Jar Was Empty

choices.text: Make the jar warm, so she knows it is allowed

effects.log: She puts her hand on the straw cap to steady herself, and it is warm, warm as a hand held out. She cries for a while. Then she lifts the cap and dips out rice for the children, and the next day, and the next. The jar goes down. You go cold.

choices.text: Keep the luck in the jar

effects.log: You go cold and hard under the jar, and she feels it, and puts the dipper down, and does not lift the cap. To eat the site's rice is to eat the house's luck, and a house with no luck in a hungry spring is a house with no tomorrow. You may be right. It does not feel like being right.

choices.text: Leave it to her

effects.log: Nothing from you, warm or cold. She stands a long time, and then she decides for herself, and lifts the cap. She takes half. She puts the cap back very carefully, and bows. It is her house. It was always her decision.

events.text: The rice from your jar keeps the children through the spring hunger, a dipperful a day boiled thin with greens. And as the jar empties you empty with it. By the time the barley is ripe there is only a handful of grains at the bottom of the jar, and you are a cold grey lump in the clay, barely more than earth.
events.arc: The Year the Jar Was Empty

choices.text: Hold on to the last handful

effects.log: They leave the last handful. Nobody tells them to; they simply do. It is enough to stay warm on, just. You come back slowly through the summer, like a field after a flood. The children are all alive. You count them every evening.

choices.text: Let them have the last handful too

effects.log: The last grains go into the last pot of the spring. For two months you are not warm at all. You are clay. You remember almost nothing of that summer except, faintly, the children's feet, getting quicker. (-8 health)

events.text: The jar stayed full through the spring hunger, and the luck stayed in it. The house was not struck by anything: no fever, no fire, no ox lost. But the children were thin as rakes, and the youngest has a cough that does not go, and the mother looks at the jar, now, the way one looks at a neighbour who did not help.
events.arc: The Year the Jar Was Empty

choices.text: Give the youngest all the warmth you kept

effects.log: All the luck you held back, at once, into one small chest. The cough breaks in a week. The mother never knows. She does not bow to the jar for a year. You think that is fair. (-5 health)

choices.text: Bear the mother's look

effects.log: You kept the house's luck whole, and the house is whole, and thin, and cold toward you. Both things are true. A centre that keeps everything safe is not always loved for it. You learn this early, under a jar, in a hungry spring.

events.text: The barley comes in at last, and the first new grain of the year goes, before anything else, into the jar behind the house. The mother pours it herself, slowly, and stands back, and looks at the jar for a long while with her hands folded.
events.arc: The Year the Jar Was Empty

choices.text: Warm the new grain at once

effects.log: Warm by the time she has taken her hands away. She nods, once, the way you nod to someone across a field after a long quarrel or a long illness. It is enough. The two of you have been through a spring together.

choices.text: Take it slowly, as earth does

effects.log: You drink the new barley the way you drink the first rain: a grain at a time, all summer. By autumn you are yourself again. The jar is warm again. The house remembers this spring for three generations, and tells it differently every time.

events.text: Debts, two bad harvests, a cousin with land in the next county. The family is selling the house. Strangers have walked round the yard twice, stamping on it and asking about the well. The ox cart is packed. On the last morning the eldest of the house stands by the jar behind the house, with the straw cap in one hand, not sure whether a spirit is a thing you take with you.

choices.text: Go with the jar

effects.log: You draw yourself up into the old rice, all of you, the whole warm clod of you, out of the clay you were born in. It is like being pulled out of a bath. The eldest feels the jar grow heavy and nearly drops it, and holds it tighter, and carries it to the cart. You go with the family.

choices.text: Stay with the site

effects.log: You stay down in the yellow clay. The jar goes onto the cart cold and light, only rice. The eldest knows. Halfway down the lane, the cart stops, and the eldest looks back at the yard for a long time, and then the cart goes on. You are the ground. The ground stays.

choices.text: Let the eldest decide

ok.log: The eldest puts the cap back on and lifts the jar, and you go up into it, because you were asked, in a way. It is the first time anyone has chosen you over a place. You remember it.

fail.log: The eldest sets the cap back on the jar and leaves it where it is. "It belongs to the site," the eldest says, to nobody. The cart goes without it. You stay under the yard with an empty jar over you, which is a new kind of cold.

events.text: The new house is in the next valley, on a slope, with a yard half the size and a well that tastes of iron. The eldest digs a hollow behind it, by the new soy-sauce jars, and sets the old jar in, and puts the straw cap on. You go down out of the rice into strange clay: red, stony, cold, and nobody's.

choices.text: Make the strange clay yours

effects.log: It takes two years. You push into the red stony ground, warming it, softening it, teaching it what a site is for. By the third tenth month the new yard is warm and the iron has gone out of the well. You are the old lord of a new site. (-3 health)

choices.text: Stay in the jar's rice and only the jar's

effects.log: You do not go down into the red clay. You stay small, in the rice, for the family only. A spirit of a jar, not of a ground. It is a quieter thing to be. It is enough for a while, and then it is not.

events.text: The strangers move in. They are loud and careful at once, the way new people in a house are. They do not know what the empty jar behind the house is for. They find it full of dust and old husks, and stand round it arguing. One wants to throw it out. One wants to use it for salt.

choices.text: Make the empty jar warm

effects.log: They feel it at once, all of them, a warmth coming out of an empty jar in the cold. Nobody uses it for salt. In the tenth month the new family fills it with their own new rice, not knowing why. You have a new house above you. The old one is gone. You are still here.

choices.text: Let them do as they like

effects.log: It becomes the salt jar. You lie under salt for a year. It is not unpleasant. Next autumn their child, poking about behind the house, finds the old straw cap rotting in the hedge, and puts it back on the jar, very seriously. Children know.

events.text: Many years later, a traveller in a good coat stops at the gate of the old house: the eldest's grandchild, grown and doing well in another county, come to see the place the family left. The traveller stands in the yard, awkward, a stranger in it, and then goes round behind the house to look for something.

choices.text: Warm the place where the old jar stood

effects.log: There is nothing there now but a hollow. The traveller kneels and puts a hand in it, and it is warm, and the traveller stays kneeling longer than a person in a good coat should. "Grandmother said you would remember," the traveller says. You do.

choices.text: Stay still, and let the family be gone

effects.log: The traveller finds the hollow cold, nods as if expecting it, and goes. You were their luck once. Now you are somebody else's. Families go. Sites stay. You have chosen which one you are, and you were not wrong.

events.text: Something is tunnelling through your yard. Ridges come up overnight in the packed clay, and molehills like little graves. Then a voice, small and very loud, from inside the earth: it is the Mole King, lord of everything underground, and this yard is part of its kingdom, and it would like you to know whose ground you are lying in.

choices.text: Ask what makes it king

effects.log: It tells you, proudly. Its grandfather went looking for the greatest groom under heaven for his daughter. The sun said the cloud was greater; the cloud said the wind; the wind said the stone Buddha in the field, whom it cannot move; and the stone Buddha said: the mole who digs under my feet. So.

choices.text: Tell it whose ground this is

effects.log: You go hard as fired brick under the next tunnel. The Mole King hits it nose first. There is a long, offended silence. Then the tunnels go round your middle in a ring, very carefully, as if that had always been the plan.
