choices.text: Laugh: a warmth through the whole yard

effects.log: The yard goes warm all at once. Somewhere inside it a small loud voice demands to know what is funny. Nothing. Everything. It is the first time you have laughed. A mole was the cause. You will never tell anyone.

events.text: The Mole King has decided that a king must have a throne room, and that the warmest spot in its kingdom is the right place for one. It is tunnelling straight for your middle, fast, with its whole court of moles behind it. If it gets there, your heart will be full of mole.

choices.text: Stop it with force

ok.log: You close the clay round the tunnel like a fist round a stick. The Mole King backs out, slowly, very dignified, covered in yellow dust. It does not apologise. It never comes nearer than the gate again.

fail.log: It is faster than you, and you are not good at fast. It reaches the warm clay at your edge and digs itself a round room there and sits in it, triumphant. You have a mole in you now. It is very annoying, and very warm. (-6 health)

choices.text: Open a warm room for it at your edge, and nowhere nearer

effects.log: You make a hollow at your very edge, warm as a hearth, and let the tunnel find it. The Mole King moves in at once and declares it the throne room of the underground. It is a mile from your heart, as moles go. Everyone is happy.

choices.text: Remind it of the stone Buddha

effects.log: "The Buddha said you dig under its feet," you tell it. "Then who digs under yours?" A long silence in the tunnel. A mole is very small, and the ground is very large, and it has never once thought of that. It turns round.

events.text: Winter. The Mole King is old, and its court is smaller, and it comes up close under the frost to talk, which a king does not usually do. It wants to know, now that it thinks about it, what is under you. Who is the greatest, really. The sun, the cloud, the wind, the stone, the mole. And under the mole?

choices.text: Tell it: the ground, and nothing is greater, and nothing is lesser

effects.log: It thinks about this all winter. In spring it says that it is a very unsatisfactory answer, and it is the right one, and it does not want to hear it again. The Mole King dies in its warm room in the next autumn, still a king.

choices.text: Tell it: the mole, of course

effects.log: It is very pleased. It tells its grandchildren. Somewhere, in a tale the old people tell, the mole is still the greatest groom under heaven. You see no reason to take that from it.

events.text: Blue fire in the yard at midnight, bobbing. Then a dokkaebi: shaggy, one horn, a knobbed club over its shoulder, and a clay pot under its arm that clinks. It looks round furtively, digs a hole in your yard with its hands, puts the pot in, fills it, stamps on it, looks round again, and goes. The coins in the pot are very cold. They are lying on your back.

choices.text: Hold the pot where it is

effects.log: It is not yours. It is not the family's. It is the dokkaebi's, and it buried it in good faith, in the best ground in the valley. You hold it still. A centre is a good place to bury things. You are beginning to understand banks.

choices.text: Let it sink deeper, where nobody will ever find it

effects.log: Down it goes, a hand at a time, all winter, until it lies at your middle like a cold stone in a warm loaf. Nobody will find it there. Including, you suspect, the dokkaebi.

choices.text: Bring it up for the family to find

effects.log: By morning a corner of the pot is showing in the yard like a mushroom. The grandfather finds it sweeping, and sits down hard, and the family pays its debts and buys a second ox. Somewhere, you suspect, there will be consequences.

events.text: The dokkaebi is back, a year later, very merry, smelling strongly of rice beer, and it cannot remember where it buried the pot. It digs a hole by the gate. It digs a hole by the well. It digs up half the yard by moonlight, singing, and then it sits down in the middle of you and offers the ground a bowl of buckwheat jelly if the ground will only tell it where.

choices.text: Tell it, and take the jelly

effects.log: A warm spot in the yard, right where it is. The dokkaebi digs, finds the pot, kisses it, and leaves the bowl of jelly on the ground, which is how you come to be the only clod in the valley ever to have been paid in buckwheat jelly. The family's hens eat it.

choices.text: Keep it hidden: it was buried with you, not given to it

effects.log: The dokkaebi digs until dawn and finds nothing, and goes off weeping and swearing to come back. The family finds the yard dug up like a ploughed field and blames the neighbour's pig. You are left holding a goblin's money. That is never simple.

choices.text: Fill in all its holes as it goes

effects.log: Every hole it digs closes behind it, so neatly that it begins to think it has not dug them at all, and starts again by the gate. It goes round the yard three times. At dawn it gives up, deeply puzzled, and leaves the yard smoother than it found it.

events.text: Dokkaebi are honest in the strangest way. The one whose pot this yard once held comes back every few years, at night, by blue fire, and leaves a handful of coins on the yard: repaying, it says, a loan. It cannot remember the loan. It cannot remember that it has repaid it eleven times. The family has stopped asking where the coins come from.

choices.text: Tell it the debt is paid

effects.log: It is shocked. It is outraged. It sits on the yard all night arguing with the ground about accounts. In the morning it goes, still muttering, and leaves one more handful, for interest. It never comes back. The family misses the coins and does not know why.

choices.text: Let it keep paying

effects.log: Every few years, a handful of coins in the yard at dawn. The family never grows rich and never quite goes hungry. The village says the house is lucky. The house is lucky. It is paying back a goblin's debt that never existed, through you. Luck is mostly like that.

events.text: A traveller in a horsehair hat and a grey robe stops at the gate and asks for water, and then does not leave. {npc} has a round wooden compass, rings and rings of tiny characters round a needle, and is walking slowly across the yard with it held out flat, the way one carries a full bowl. In the middle of the yard {he} stops. The needle is shivering.

choices.text: Hold the needle still for {him}

effects.log: The needle stops dead. {npc} looks at it, and at the mountains, all of them, one after another, all round the valley, and says to the farmer on the porch: "Do you know what you are standing on? The navel of the valley. Everything here leans to this spot." The farmer does not know what to do with this.

choices.text: Make the needle spin

effects.log: Round and round. {npc} goes pale, then pink, then sits down in the middle of the yard with the compass in both hands, laughing. "Something is here," {he} tells the farmer. "Something big. Do not ever sell this house." The farmer has been thinking about selling the house.

choices.text: Stay cold and ordinary

effects.log: The needle settles, a little uncertain. {npc} frowns, turns round twice, and walks the yard again. At the end {he} shrugs and goes. But {he} comes back to the gate before the bend in the road, and looks at the yard once more, and writes something down.

events.text: {npc}, the geomancer, is back, and not alone: with a rich buyer in silk from the county town, whose old father is dying and needs the best grave in the valley. A grave on the navel of the valley, {npc} has promised, will make that family great for nine generations. The buyer is offering the farmer more silver than the farmer has ever seen.

choices.text: Make the ground bitter to the rich man

effects.log: The buyer stands on the yard with aching feet and aching teeth, and cannot say why, and goes away calling the geomancer a fool. {npc} goes away saying nothing, and looking back. The farmer keeps the house and does not know whether to be glad.

choices.text: Let the farmer choose

effects.log: The farmer looks at the silver a long time. Then the farmer looks at the jar behind the house, and the children on the yard, and says no. The buyer laughs and goes. You did nothing at all, and it went the way you would have chosen. You suspect that will not always happen.

choices.text: Tell the geomancer the truth, through the needle

ok.log: The needle swings, slowly, away from the yard and out over the village, toward the place below it where the five roads meet. {npc} follows it with {his} eyes and goes very still. "Not here," {he} says at last. "It is moving." {He} sends the buyer away.

fail.log: The needle only shivers. {npc} cannot read it and will not lie about it, which you respect. The buyer goes away to find a grave somewhere else. The farmer keeps the house. Nobody learns anything, which is restful.

events.text: {npc} comes back one last time, old now, with a map: the whole valley painted on mulberry paper, every ridge and stream, with all the lines of the land drawn in fine red ink. They all run to one spot. {He} has marked it with a small yellow circle, and the circle is not over this yard any more. It is a little way off, where the village road meets four others.

choices.text: Agree with the map

effects.log: The yard is warm under the old geomancer's feet, all of it, and warmer toward the gate, and warmest toward the crossroads. {npc} rolls up the map. "You are growing," {he} says to the ground. "I will tell nobody. They will find out." {He} goes down the road to the crossroads and stands there till dark.

choices.text: Ask the map how it knows

effects.log: Lines of water, lines of ridge, the way the wind goes round the hills, the old roads that follow them. {npc} explains it all to the yard, at length, as old people do. You understand perhaps a third. It is enough. The navel of the valley is where everything meets. And you are moving toward it.

events.text: You do not fit any more. Your edges have gone out under the wall and the hedge, under the neighbour's vegetable patch and the lane, and the house above you is a small thing on a wide warm back. Some nights you feel the lane's far end, where it meets the village road, and the road where it meets others, as clearly as you feel the jar.

choices.text: Stretch toward the road

effects.log: Under the lane, under the ditch, toward the road. The cart wheels on it go over your edge now. You feel strangers, all day, coming and going. It is too much, and then it is not enough.

choices.text: Draw yourself in, back under the yard

effects.log: You pull your edges in, tight, back under the house you know. It is warm and small and safe. It is also, you realise, a little too small. You are growing whether you allow it or not.

events.text: Below the village, where the lane comes down, five roads meet: from the hills, the river, the county town, the pass, and the sea. All day the feet go over that spot from five directions, and all day you feel it pulling, the way the jar's rice pulled at you once, and the yellow stripe on a child's sleeve. The centre of something larger is calling.

choices.text: Go when you are ready

effects.log: Not yet. Soon. You leave a warm root under the jar behind the house, the way you once left one under the yard, and you begin, a hand's width a year, to move down the lane toward the crossroads. The family above you never notices. That is right.

choices.text: Promise the house one more harvest first

effects.log: One more harvest. The best in a generation, flails going all day, the chaff gold in the wind. Then you go. In the tenth month the new rice goes into the jar as always, and is warm as always, a little less warm than it was. Enough.

choices.text: Ask the five roads what they want

effects.log: Nothing. They want nothing. They meet. That is all a crossroads is: the place where the ways that do not agree come together and go on. You think you could do that. You think, in a way, you always have.

events.text: Somebody dug here in the dead days, in a life that was not yours: a family's new house that had to stand before the autumn rains. The spade came up full of yellow clay that was warm, and something in it beat. That something was you, or will be, or is. The family of the spade is the family above you now. They do not remember. The ground does.

choices.text: Forgive the spade

effects.log: They were afraid of the rain, and they had children, and the old rules are old. You forgive the spade before anyone asks. It is easy, when you are clay: forgiving is only lying still and staying warm.

choices.text: Remember it, and be warm anyway

effects.log: You keep the memory of the spade the way a field keeps the memory of the plough: as the reason it is soft. The family above you will never be unlucky for it. They will never be told it either.

events.text: Somebody waited the eighteen days, in a life that was not yours, and lost a house to the autumn rains for it, rather than dig in the dead days. When at last they dug, the clay under the site was warm. You are born in that warmth. Some part of you knows it is owed to somebody's wet, roofless autumn.

choices.text: Owe it, gladly

effects.log: A debt that cannot be paid back can still be paid forward. You decide, as a clod decides anything, that every house ever built on you will be dry before the first rain.

choices.text: Lie very still for eighteen days in their honour

effects.log: Eighteen days without stirring. When the season turns you feel you have understood something about patience that most things learn too late, and that somebody learned for you.

events.text: A jar of new rice with a straw cap, buried by a shaman's word over a house site, in a life that was not yours, "so whatever lives there has a roof". You were born under a roof before you were born at all. The first thing you ever knew was that somebody, unasked, made room for you.

choices.text: Make room for somebody, one day

effects.log: You do not know who, or when. You put the promise at your middle with everything else. It is the warmest thing there.

choices.text: Feel for the shape of the old jar

effects.log: There is nothing there but clay. There is, if you lie still enough, the faint round print of something that once sat over you, the way a pillow keeps a head. You sleep in it.

events.text: Someone stood in an empty centre, in a life that was not yours, and held everything that leaned on it for half a season, and then set it down and said so: I cannot carry this to the end, and I will not pretend I can. You are born light. Nothing is owed. The groove in you is shallow and clean, as if somebody swept it.

choices.text: Be grateful for the honesty

effects.log: It is harder to set a thing down and say so than to hold it and be praised. Whoever it was did the harder thing. You start your life with nothing on your back, and you know whose doing that is, a little.

choices.text: Promise to say so too, when the time comes

effects.log: One day something will be too heavy. You decide, now, in the warm dark, that when that day comes you will say so out loud. It is an odd thing for a clod to decide. It is the right thing.

events.text: A child of the house stamps on the yard. Not playing: stamping, hard, twice, the way the band does at the first full moon, and then stands very still with both fists clenched, waiting. As if the child knew, from somewhere, that a yard can stamp back. Somebody, in a life that was not yours, stamped twice on a yard and was answered.

choices.text: Stamp back

effects.log: Once, from below, under the small bare feet. The child does not scream. The child laughs, the high astonished laugh of somebody proved right, and runs to tell everyone, and nobody believes it, and the child does not care at all.

choices.text: Warm the ground instead, gently

effects.log: Not a stamp: a warmth, spreading out under the child's feet like a hand opened. The child stops waiting, and sits down on the warm spot, and stays there all afternoon, satisfied, as if that were the answer expected all along.

events.text: A child lies down flat on the yard with one ear to the packed clay and holds very still, for a long time, the way nobody has ever taught a child to. Listening. Somebody, in a life that was not yours, lay down on a yard like this and heard it breathe. The habit has come down to this child the way a tune comes down a family.

choices.text: Breathe, slowly, so the child can hear

effects.log: In, a long time. Out, a long time. The child's eyes go very wide and then very calm. The child will grow up never quite able to be afraid of the dark, because the dark, it turns out, is breathing.

choices.text: Hold your breath, so the child gets up and plays

effects.log: Nothing. The child listens, frowns, gets up, and goes off to play tops with the others. Some things are better found later. You will breathe for this one some other year.

events.text: New Year's day, and a child of the house, alone in the yard, breaks a rice cake in half and pushes one half down into a crack in the frozen clay, and pats it, and says: there, that is for you. Somebody, in a life that was not yours, gave a New Year rice cake to the ground. It was the first gift you were ever given that was not owed.

choices.text: Take the gift

effects.log: It is sweet and cold and a little dirty. It is the best thing you have ever eaten, because nobody had to. By the next morning the crack has closed over it, smooth, and the child checks, and is deeply satisfied.

choices.text: Give the child a good year back

effects.log: Half a rice cake, a year without a single fever or a fall or a lost top. The child never connects the two. You do. You keep the account very carefully, and you are still in the child's debt.
